title: A B2B Customer Onboarding Checklist with Owners and Exit Criteria
summary: A customer onboarding checklist should tell people what to do, who owns the work, and what counts as complete.
body_markdown:
A customer onboarding checklist should tell people what to do, who owns the work, and what counts as complete. A list of activities without exit criteria can make an account look busy while leaving the customer unable to achieve the intended outcome.


Use the checklist below as a starting point for B2B onboarding. Adapt it to your product and implementation requirements. It is an operational template, not a claim that every customer should follow the same timeline.


## The checklist


Stage Task Owner to name Completion evidence


Before kickoff Accept the sales handoff Onboarding owner Goals, scope, promises, and questions reviewed


Before kickoff Confirm customer contacts Relationship owner Sponsor and working contacts identified


Before kickoff Record first-value milestone Both sides Written agreement on the desired result


Kickoff Agree responsibilities Onboarding owner Named owner for each dependency


Kickoff Confirm communication route Both sides Customer knows where to ask for help


Preparation Verify access Technical owner Intended users can access the required environment


Preparation Validate required inputs Relevant specialist Inputs meet the agreed requirements


Preparation Resolve scope questions Authorised decision-maker Decision recorded and communicated


First workflow Complete a representative task Customer user Customer performs the workflow with appropriate help


First workflow Review the result Both sides Output meets agreed acceptance criteria


Adoption Confirm repeatability Customer owner Customer can repeat the workflow


Transition Assign remaining work Sending and receiving owners Every open item has an accepted owner


Transition Introduce ongoing support Relationship owner Customer knows the next contact and review point


Do not mark a task complete because an email was sent unless sending the email is the actual obligation. Access is complete when the required user can use it, not when an invitation has been generated.


## Add fields that prevent ambiguity


Each checklist item should have a due date or review point, a state, an owner, and an evidence link. A dependency field explains why the task cannot yet proceed. A changed-plan note preserves the reason an item was cancelled or revised.


Use a small set of states consistently. Open, in progress, blocked, complete, and cancelled are usually enough to start. “Blocked” should require a reason and a next review point. “Complete” should refer to observable evidence.


Avoid separate copies in several tools. If a customer-facing checklist and an internal checklist are both necessary, define which record owns the state and how the other stays accurate.


## Adapt the checklist by complexity


A straightforward onboarding may combine several tasks into one session. A complex implementation may split preparation into security review, data readiness, integration work, and testing. Add detail where it changes responsibility or reduces risk.


Do not add tasks merely because they appear in another company’s template. Every item should support the customer’s objective, a genuine implementation requirement, or an agreed service obligation. Unnecessary tasks slow the process and make the important items harder to see.


Use the[onboarding plan template](https://o11.ai/blog/customer-onboarding-plan-template) to describe the higher-level milestones. The checklist should explain execution beneath those milestones rather than duplicate the entire plan.


## An illustrative blocker


Suppose the customer cannot invite the second team. The checklist item is “Verify access for the rollout group.” It remains blocked, with the issue linked and a support owner named. The next review point is the promised support update.


Training should not silently move forward as if access were complete. Either revise the session to address preparation that can happen without access, or agree a new date. Record that decision so the next person understands why the schedule changed.


This example shows why dependencies matter. A simple incomplete checkbox does not explain whether the team should send a reminder, fix a problem, or change the plan.


## Run a short operational review


Review the checklist around decisions: what is overdue, what is blocked, what has changed, and what the customer needs next. Do not read every completed item aloud. Focus attention on work that requires an owner or a decision.


Check a sample of completed tasks against their evidence. This discourages premature completion and reveals unclear definitions. If people interpret a task differently, improve the wording rather than treating every disagreement as a performance issue.


Keep the customer informed about meaningful changes. They do not need every internal task, but they should understand the milestones, their responsibilities, and any change that affects the outcome.


## Graduate with a clear handoff


Before closing onboarding, confirm the first-value milestone and identify any remaining work. An account can transition with open items if their ownership is explicit and the customer understands the plan. It should not transition simply because the original target date has arrived.


Our[implementation-to-account-management handoff](https://o11.ai/blog/implementation-to-account-management-handoff) explains how to preserve the remaining context. The checklist is complete when it supports a reliable transition, not when every inconvenient item has been removed.


For another reference, see[Rocketlane’s onboarding checklist](https://blog.rocketlane.com/blogs/client-onboarding-checklist) . To explore how o11 can support customer context and next steps within your checklist,[bring one workflow to a demo](https://o11.ai/demo) .
